Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:54: We shall proceed to explain, in a chapter of its own, how great is the level of one who guards his mouth and tongue, and how great the blemish, even though we have already explained something of this in this chapter — in the next chapter we shall add further teaching, please God. We have divided the matter into its own chapter to give the student some breathing room between chapters.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:1: It is written, "Who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good? Guard your tongue from evil..." (Psalms 34:13). Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 19a, near the end): Rabbi Alexandri would proclaim, "Who wants life? Who wants life?" And the whole world would gather to him; they would say to him, "Give us life!" He would say to them, "'Who is the man who desires life...' guard your tongue... turn from evil and do good." Lest a person say, "I have guarded my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit," [and think this suffices, and] indulge in sleep [i.e., idleness] — the verse teaches, "turn from evil and do good," and "good" refers only to Torah, as it is said, "for I give you good instruction; do not forsake My Torah" (Proverbs 4:2) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:2: This story is brought in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 16:2) in a different manner, and my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote that what it says — that [Rabbi Alexandri] understood the verse only through that peddler — is because the verse is doubled: it says "who is the man who desires life" and then repeats, "who loves days to see good." This is resolved through the peddler proclaiming, "Who wants life?" — for the whole world came to him — [teaching] that if for the life of this world a person pursues obtaining a remedy through which he may live, all the more so should he pursue the life of the World to Come; and the days that should love him, for the rectification of his soul, he should not sin in them through his tongue, so that they not turn into enemies and accusers against him. This is [the meaning of] "loves days" — that the days themselves should love him, for his good, in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:3: And in the Zohar (Parashat Shemini 41a) this verse is explained, in these words: Rabbi Abba opened and said, "Who is the man who desires life... guard your tongue from evil..." and it is written, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue..." (Proverbs 21:23). "Who is the man who desires life" — what is "life"? Rather, this is the life called the World to Come, and life dwells there; and therefore we have learned, "she is a tree of life" (Proverbs 3:18) — a tree from that life, a tree planted in that life; and therefore it is written, "Who is the man who desires life." "Who loves days to see good" — what are "days"? Rather, this is the Name of the holy King that is bound to those supernal days called "the days of heaven upon the earth" (Deuteronomy 11:21) — "the days of heaven," certainly, "upon the earth," certainly. Whoever wants the life above, to have a portion in it, and whoever wants the days, to be attached to them and to love them, let him guard his mouth from everything — let him guard his mouth from eating and drinking that defiles the soul, and let him distance himself from those life and those days. Let him guard his mouth from evil words, so as not to become defiled by them, and let him distance himself from them and have no portion in them. Come and see, mouth and tongue are likewise called a supernal place; therefore a person should not blemish his mouth and tongue, and all the more so should he not defile his own soul and body, since he becomes defiled in another world — this has already been established.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:4: What appears to us in explaining the verse according to the plain sense, in saying "who is the man (ish)" — in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, end of 128a) it explains that whoever overcomes his inclination is called "ish." The reason one who guards his tongue from evil is called "ish" is that the sin of the tongue is constant, and one who overcomes his inclination and does not speak when his inclination entices him to speak deserves to be called "ish" — unlike other transgressions, which, even though he may occasionally succumb to them, are not so common, and do not give as great a stature to be called "ish" as one who guards his tongue does.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:5: The intent is to tell us the great level a person attains by properly guarding the tongue. First, the cause of attachment to his God, as explained — that this is the essential life, and therefore the righteous person is called "living" — "and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, son of a living man" (II Samuel 23:20), and likewise, "let the living take it to heart" (Ecclesiastes 7:2), and as the liturgical poet said, "in my distance from You is my death in my life; and if I cleave to You, my life is in my death." What follows from one's desiring life is that he "loves days" — for the days are supernal illuminations drawn down below for the rectification of the soul, and the hidden reward reserved for the righteous is hidden and concealed within the days; and whoever refines himself merits to see his world in his lifetime, as they said (Berachot 17a), "you shall see your world in your lifetime" — this is [the meaning of] "to see good" — meaning, to see his world in his lifetime — and only one who guards his tongue properly attains this level. This is what the passage says: "your mouth shall speak wisdom and your tongue shall whisper songs of joy," and everything mentioned in the passage is a preparation for what is stated at the beginning of the passage: "you shall see your world in your lifetime, and your hope [shall be] for the world of worlds."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:6: It says, "guard your tongue from evil (ra)" — agreed upon in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, beginning of 57), that the word "ra" applies to one who emits seed in vain, and he supports the matter from the verse, "and Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil (ra) in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 38:7) — meaning that he emitted seed in vain. In these words, briefly, on this matter: Rabbi Yosei said, is not "ra" [simply] "rasha" (wicked)? He said to him, no — a "rasha" is even one who raises his hand against his fellow, even though he does nothing to him, is called "rasha," as it is written, "and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow?" (Exodus 2:13) — it does not say "you struck" but "do you strike" [in the ongoing/potential sense]; but "ra" is called only one who corrupts his way and defiles himself and defiles the earth — so far his words, as pertains to us. This makes explicit, in negative form, that "ra" is called only [one who does thus], and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:7: Now, in this same manner the tongue must be explained; the matter is that, having explained that there are two covenants corresponding to one another — the covenant of the tongue and the covenant of the sexual organ (Sefer Yetzirah 1:2) — just as, regarding the covenant of the sexual organ, one who emits seed in vain is called "ra," so regarding the covenant of the tongue, one who utters a word in vain is like one who emits seed in vain; therefore it says, "guard your tongue from evil (ra)," so that you not be called "ra," which is one who "emits" as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:8: It says "netzor" (guard, in an intensive form) and not "shemor" (guard, simple form) or the like, to indicate a great guarding, a fence and wall within a wall, as the word "netzor" indicates. And so the Radak explains in Sefer HaShorashim, that "netzor" is from the root of "matzor" (siege/fortification), as in "and you shall build a fortification against the city" (Deuteronomy 20:20), which is the finest form of guarding.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:9: Likewise, the wording "netzor leshoncha" ("guard your tongue") — it does not say "guard the tongue from evil," but "your tongue" — meaning that you should see with the eye of the intellect that your tongue is surrounded by two walls, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Arachin 15b), on the verse, "What shall he give unto you, and what shall he add unto you, you deceitful tongue?" (Psalms 120:3): the Holy One, blessed be He, said to the tongue: all of a person's limbs stand upright, but you lie flat; all of a person's limbs are on the outside, but you are on the inside; and not only that, but I have surrounded you with two walls, one of bone and one of flesh — "what shall he give unto you," and so on — so far his words. This is the matter of "netzor," alluding to a hidden and concealed place, to indicate the fortification of the two walls it has — that the Creator concealed it with these hidden walls, which He did not do for the other limbs, and this is certainly because of its greatness, like the parable of a man who stores, in a treasury within a treasury, the precious thing he possesses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:10: To explain why one who emits seed in vain and one who utters a word in vain are both called "ra," the reason is what we have explained — that the tongue is in the place of "life," as explained above regarding "who is the man who desires life"; and just as the seed is a person's physical vitality — it is "the light of his eyes," and so on (Rambam, Hilchot De'ot 4:19) — and it engenders physically, as is known, and one who emits it in vain is called "ra" because of the mystery and allusion in it above, so too the word of the tongue, which is a fortification of the mystery of spiritual vitality clothed in the vessel of the tongue, engenders above in spiritual holiness, and it is not fitting that it go forth in vain — and this is the greatness of Rav [Yehudah], who never in his life spoke idle talk.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:11: Although we have said that idle speech is called "ra," nevertheless any speech that is blemished and indicates an "outsider" is likewise called "ra" — the proof being evil speech (lashon hara), which is harmful, and even though some benefit may come from saying it, nevertheless it is called "ra" of itself, since the outsider has a part in it. The general principle of "guard your tongue" is [to guard it] from any speech in which the outsider, called "ra," has a part.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:12: It says "your tongue" and "your lips," using the second-person form of address, indicating what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Bereshit Rabbah (67:3), that the mouth is at a person's discretion — that if he wishes he can speak Torah and good, and if he wishes he can speak evil — this being "your tongue" and "your lips," which are at your discretion. In these words: Rabbi Levi said, six things serve a person, three at his discretion and three not at his discretion. The ear, the nose, and the eye are not at his discretion — he sees what he does not want, hears what he does not want, smells what he does not want. The mouth, the hand, and the foot are at his discretion — if he wishes he studies Torah, if he wishes he blasphemes, if he wishes he does not blaspheme. The hand — if he wishes he distributes charity, if he wishes he steals and kills. The foot — if he wishes he goes to synagogues and study halls, if he wishes he goes to theaters and circuses. At a time when a person is meritorious, the Holy One, blessed be He, makes what is at his discretion not at his discretion: the mouth — "and he shall also be blessed" (Genesis 27:33) [an involuntary blessing]; the hand — "and his hand dried up" (I Kings 13:4); the foot — "my son, do not walk in the way with them" (Proverbs 1:15) [an involuntary restraint] — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:13: <b>Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in the book Menorat HaMa'or that there are seven openings in the head, corresponding to the seven branches of the Menorah, and the mouth corresponds to the middle branch, which is holy; therefore one must sanctify his mouth and tongue on the day of Shabbat, which is the seventh and holy, since all sevenths are holy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:14: And in the Tikkunim (137a): "the Torah of truth was in his mouth" (Malachi 2:6) — this is the Sanctuary (Heichal), and concerning it is said, "O Lord, open my lips" (Psalms 51:17); within it, the Holy of Holies, which is the heart — so far his words. It stands to reason that one should sanctify speech, since it emerges from the Holy of Holies, which is the heart, into the Sanctuary, which is the mouth. Further, you will find that the word "kadosh" (holy) by the small reckoning, with the four letters counted, equals the numerical value of "dibbur" (speech) by the small reckoning.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:15: Further, "guard your tongue from evil" means that one who blemishes his mouth with words of vulgarity and the like becomes defiled and comes to emit seed in vain, to teach him that this is "evil," as is explained in the Zohar (Introduction, 8a), on the verse, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" (Ecclesiastes 5:5), in these words: Rav Hamnuna Sabba said, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" — that a person not give his mouth to come to an evil fantasy, causing that holy flesh, sealed with the holy Covenant, to sin; for if he does so, they draw him to Gehinnom, and the one appointed over Gehinnom is called Duma, and there are many myriads of destroying angels with him, standing at the gate of Gehinnom; and all who guard the holy Covenant in this world, he has no permission to approach them — so far his words. My teacher, peace be upon him, was precise about the wording "that a person not give his mouth to come to...," that the intent is to be precise about the wording of the verse, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" — for the intent is not to warn us only against sinning with the tongue, for then it should have said "do not sin with your mouth"; rather, even things that do not involve vulgar speech, but that lead to fantasy, are forbidden — such as speaking to one's wife about matters of intimacy, which may lead to fantasy and cause his flesh, which is a holy covenant, to sin by emitting seed in vain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:16: It follows from this that guarding the Covenant depends on guarding the tongue, since they are two corresponding covenants, as explained; and therefore the verse gives priority to guarding the tongue, because it is the essential thing, included in the two hundred (i.e., it is the more fundamental of the two) — for if he guards the tongue, the Covenant is automatically guarded, but if he is not careful to guard the tongue while being careful to guard the Covenant, even his guarding of the Covenant does not stand for him — the reason being as we have explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:17: And so it is likewise explained in Parashat Noach and Parashat Acharei Mot, that one who blemishes with his tongue is defiled, and is found to be called "ra." At the end of Parashat Noach (76a) it says, in these words: Rabbi Yosei opened and said, "For the Lord your God walks (mit'halech) in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you; therefore shall your camp be holy, that He see no unclean thing (ervat davar) in you, and turn away from you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). "For the Lord your God walks" — it should have said "walks" (mehalech, simple form); rather, as it is said, "walking (mit'halech) in the garden in the cool of the day" (Genesis 3:8), which refers to the tree from which Adam ate. "Mit'halech" is female, "mehalech" is male; and this is what goes before Israel when they walked in the desert, as it is written, "and the Lord went before them by day..." (Exodus 13:21); this is what goes before a person when he walks on the road, as it is written, "righteousness shall go before Him, and shall set his footsteps on the way" (Psalms 85:14); and this is what goes before a person at the time he is meritorious. And why? "To deliver you and to give up your enemies" — to save a person on the road and let no other rule over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:18: Therefore a person must guard himself from his sins and purify himself — what is "purify"? "Therefore shall your camp be holy (kadosh)" — what is "kadosh"? It should have said "kedoshim" [plural, since "camp" collectively includes many]; rather, "your camp shall be holy" refers to those limbs of the body, that the body be joined and rectified through them, and therefore "your camp shall be holy." "That He see no unclean thing (ervat davar) in you" — what is "ervat davar"? This is the nakedness of forbidden relations, for this is a matter the Holy One, blessed be He, despises more than anything. Since it says "that He see no ervah in you," why [does it add] "davar" (a word/matter)? Rather, these are the wicked of the world who defile and pollute themselves through their own speech that emerges from their mouths, and this is "ervat davar" ("nakedness of a word"); and why all this? Because He goes before you, and if you act thus, immediately "and turn away from you" — that He not go with you, but turn away from behind you — so far his words. And so in Vayikra Rabbah (Parashat Kedoshim 24:7): "that He see no ervat davar in you" — "ervat dibbur" (nakedness of speech) — Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said, this refers to vulgar speech — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:19: And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot 75b) it says: we have learned, there are two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all become defiled when it becomes defiled — meaning, when it is [about] to become defiled; and therefore "your camp shall be holy" — what is "your camp"? These are the limbs of the body; "that He see no ervat davar in you" — what is "ervat davar"? The nakedness of this "davar" (word) — a hint, as we have established, and so on — so far his words. We quoted the rest of this passage in the Gate of Awe, chapter 5 — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:20: When we combine these two passages, our intent emerges clearly in explanation: that according to both explanations, "your camp shall be holy" refers to the two hundred forty-eight limbs — for "machaneicha" ("your camp") is mentioned in a form suggesting plurality [collectively], to indicate the two hundred forty-eight limbs. And what is said in Parashat Noach — that "ervat davar" is "ervat dibbur" (the nakedness of speech) — and what is said in Parashat Acharei Mot — that "ervat davar" is the Shechinah — are one and the same, for whoever blemishes the nakedness of speech blemishes her, since speech comes from her — and this is what the passage begins by saying, "for the Lord your God walks" [reading "mit'halech," feminine] — this is the female [Shechinah].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:21: We are forced to say, according to our approach, that "your camp shall be holy" refers to the two hundred forty-eight [limbs], and that "He walks in the midst of your camp" refers likewise to the camp of the body — for the entirety of the two hundred forty-eight are one camp, in which the neshamah rests; and since the neshamah comes from the Atzilut of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and it walks within the body — the neshamah has no life to bring forth the power of speech except according to what the Shechinah bestows, for the neshamah is a thread drawn from above from these two attributes, as it says, "for the Lord's portion is His people" (Deuteronomy 32:9), and it is impossible to separate the part from its source — it follows that, since the neshamah is below, "the Lord your God" is literally "walking in the midst of your camp" — this being "the Lord your God" — the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, from whom the neshamah's Atzilut comes, and they are voice and speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:22: The reason it says "mit'halech" and not "mehalech" is that speech is the essential thing in a person, and the voice is subordinate to it, therefore it says "mit'halech" [feminine, for the Shechinah, who governs speech]. Likewise, the place of the neshamah's gestation is within her, and she is the mother who bears it, and she raises the children — therefore she is the essential thing regarding this. Therefore it says, "that He see no ervat davar in you" — that the Shechinah, who walks within your midst, in the manner explained that she is the neshamah, and so on, should not see him waste her strength in vain and in a place of nakedness — namely, speech. Therefore it says that "ervat dibbur" is more repugnant than anything, because it is a blemish to the Shechinah and to the neshamah in a spiritual aspect — for speech is more spiritual than deed, as explained above regarding "who is the man who desires life."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:23: It says, "and your camp shall be holy" — that the two hundred forty-eight limbs should be on the side of holiness and not become defiled — as it says in Parashat Acharei Mot, "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, all of which become defiled" — and there is no sin that defiles all two hundred forty-eight limbs like the sin of a seminal emission, for the seed goes forth from all two hundred forty-eight limbs, and they all become defiled by the spirit of impurity from Lilith resting upon him. By this, the matter of "that He see no ervat davar in you" is precise — meaning, He should not see, in you, in your body, an ervat davar; for when the Shechinah is blemished, which you have blemished, the blemish upon her shows in your body, and the nakedness, which is Lilith, "ervat davar," rests upon you; and then the Shechinah withdraws from you — this being "and turn away from you" — "for evil (ra) shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:24: There is proof for this explanation in Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Zavim (18:4), which asks: from where did Israel become liable to zivah (a discharge) and tzara'at (leprosy)? Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya said, because they used to disparage their leaders, saying, "this family of so-and-so, is it not a family of lepers?" — teaching that plagues come only because of evil speech (lashon hara). Rabbi Tanchuma said, because they used to disparage the Ark, saying, "this Ark kills those who carry it," and plagues come only because of evil speech — therefore Israel became liable to zivah and tzara'at — so far his words. This makes explicit that zivah came upon them through the blemish of evil speech. Now, zivah is a blemish of the Covenant, and my teacher, peace be upon him, explains that "zav" numerically equals nine, since its blemish is in the Righteous One, the ninth attribute [Yesod]; and likewise regarding a seminal emission, whose blemish is in the Covenant, as we shall elaborate in its place — the cause of it is the blemish of the tongue through evil speech, and the other things that blemish the tongue.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:25: And so it is explained in Parashat Metzora (53a), whose wording we shall quote below: Rabbi Chiya said, whoever utters evil speech, all his limbs become defiled, and so on — this is in the manner of "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, all of which become defiled," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:26: Further, "that He see no ervat davar in you" might be explained as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso 121b) — and this is close to the previous approach — in these words: come and see, at the hour people sleep and taste the taste of death, and the neshamah ascends above, it stands in the place where it stands, and is examined regarding the deeds it did every day, and they are written on a note. Why? Because the neshamah ascends above and testifies concerning a person's deeds and concerning every single word that emerges from his mouth — for that word a person utters from his mouth ascends and bursts through the firmaments, and stands in the place it stands, until night comes and the neshamah ascends and takes hold of that word and brings it before the King — this is what is written, "from her who lies in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth" (Micah 7:5) — and then that word and that sin are marked upon that person; and therefore, "Fortunate is the man to whom the Lord does not reckon iniquity" (Psalms 32:2) — when is this? When there is no deceit in his spirit — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:27: Here it says that word is marked and that sin is upon that person — this is explained by what is known: that sins, some are marked and written on the skin of the flesh visibly, some on the forehead, and some a person's sins are engraved on his bones, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain — and this is [the meaning of] "marked upon that person": upon him literally is marked the sin of that speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:28: Even though he did not perform a deed, nevertheless speech is more severe than deed, as is explained in the Mishnah (Arachin 3:5): it follows that one who speaks with his mouth is worse than one who performs a deed, for we find that the decree against our forefathers in the desert was sealed only because of evil speech (lashon hara), as it is said, "and they have tested Me..." (Numbers 14:22). We learn from here that if he thought in his mind to commit a transgression and made up his mind to do it, and uttered that decision with his lips, it is accounted before Him, blessed be He, as though he had done it — for speech is accounted like deed, as the Mishnah says. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 40a) that it is only when a person thinks to commit a transgression and does not commit it that it is not accounted to him — but only when he has not spoken; this is [the meaning of] "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard" (Psalms 66:18) — but if I had spoken it with my lips, the Lord would have heard. And as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Emor 105a) regarding speech on Shabbat, that speech is forbidden because the voice immediately ascends above, whereas mere fantasy is permitted. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains in the Idra of Ha'azinu (294a), in the rectification of the ears — see there. And as explained in the preceding chapter on the verse, "al tevahel al picha," and so on — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:29: By this we understand "that He see no ervat davar in you" — meaning, He should see [i.e., not see] that the nakedness of that speech becomes portrayed and marked upon him, in his body — this being "in you": literally in your body it is marked; and when the body is blemished through transgression, it has a defect, and the Shechinah withdraws from it — this is "and turn away from you," for "whatever has a blemish shall not come near" (Leviticus 21:18).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:30: Further, "that He see no [ervat davar] in you" (bach) might be explained in the manner explained in the Zohar (Tosefta, Shir HaShirim, 68a) regarding "let us rejoice and be glad in you (bach)" (Song of Songs 1:4) — that "bach" [Bet-Kaf] numerically equals 22 letters, and "bo" (Bet-Vav) is Tiferet. It is known that the twenty-two letters of the Torah are marked in a person's mouth, as explained above regarding "al tevahel al picha," being Aleph-Het-Ayin-Heh in the throat, and so on. The intent is: He should not see, "in you" (bach) — should not see the Torah, which is fixed in your mouth in twenty-two letters, that you utter its letters to speak nakedness — for by this he is found to blemish the five supernal points of articulation, which are the source of the twenty-two letters. And when one considers the allusion of each and every point of articulation and where its supernal allusion lies, he will see how great the blemish of the tongue is: the thing alluded to and visible in a person's mouth is that there are thirty-two teeth, corresponding to the thirty-two paths of Chochmah, which are the thirty-two [mentions of] "Elohim" in the account of Creation, and this is one of the points of articulation, Zayin-Tzadi-Samech-Reish-Shin, in the teeth; and likewise the other points of articulation, Aleph-Het-Ayin-Heh in the throat, and the throat is more internal, so the blemish is greater; and likewise for the other points of articulation — the blemish is found in all of them at once. Therefore it says, "that He see no [ervat davar] in you (bach)" — that is, the twenty-two letters that are in the five points of articulation — "ervat davar" — that a blemish of the nakedness of speech be found in them. This is likewise the mystery of Tiferet, called "bo" (Bet-Vav) — comprised of the twenty-two letters of the Torah — He should not see ervat davar, which is His Shechinah, for when He sees the Shechinah blemished, He withdraws — this being "and turn away from you" — that mercy withdraws from him, in the manner explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 5.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:31: Now, in all the explanations given for this verse, we can understand what the Tanna says (Avot 1:17): "All my days I grew up among the Sages, and I have found nothing..." and so on. In saying "all my days I grew up," the intent is that every person, according to the place he grows up in, so he learns his traits, whether for good or the reverse; therefore he says that he grew up among the Sages, and what he learned from them is that he found nothing better than silence — for among the Sages, one must necessarily find this quality, since they said (Avot 5:7) seven things characterize a wise man, and so on: a wise man does not speak in front of one greater than him in wisdom, and does not interrupt his fellow's words, and all the other qualities mentioned regarding a sage are rooted in silence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:32: "I have found nothing better for the body (guf) than silence" — what has the body to do with this? It should have said, "I have found nothing better than silence" [without "for the body"]. Rather, the matter, according to our explanation, is that the two hundred forty-eight limbs become defiled; the intent is: I have found no purification for the body better than silence — and I found support for this explanation in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 16:5), which we quoted in chapter 13, "[do not let your mouth] cause your flesh to sin" — do not give permission to one of your limbs to cause all your limbs to sin. Or, according to the explanation that the blemish is marked on his body, if he does not sin with his mouth and is silent, certainly that sin will not be marked on his body, and mercy will not withdraw from him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:33: Or one might say, "I have found nothing for the body (guf)" means: for matters of the body, silence is good, but for words of Torah one must speak, in the manner of "the mute one of righteousness" explained above. Further, [it might refer] to the body in the manner explained in the Midrash regarding "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" (Proverbs 18:21), through the parable of the lion, as they say in the Midrash (Yalkut Tehillim, remez 721).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:34: Further, I found in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu that a certain man, after he passed away, was found by the gravediggers in the field, in his grave, alive, since the worm did not rule over him; and Rav Nachman asked him for what reason he had merited this, and he answered that he had no jealousy and did not incline his ear to hear idle words — we quoted this passage in the Gate of Humility, chapter 3, and at the end of the passage it says, "and this, when his only merit was the reward of silence alone..." and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:35: Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, in the book Menorat HaMa'or, offers another explanation, in these words: I have found no remedy for the body except silence — for whoever multiplies words is not saved from sin, and will be stricken with tzara'at in his body. And in light of what Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Zohar Parashat Mishpatim 122a), in these words: we have learned, it is written, "guard your tongue from evil (mera)" — what is "mera"? Because of evil speech, illnesses (mar'in) descend upon the world — so far his words — we explain "I have found nothing for the body" to mean that he be saved from evil illnesses, not specifically tzara'at as [Rabbi Yisrael] explains, but rather it refers to all illnesses. "But silence" — through which he is saved — and this is a great virtue of silence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:36: And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Metzora 16:5): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a word is worth a sela, silence is worth two, for we have learned, his son Shimon says: all my days I grew up among the Sages, and I have found nothing better for the body than silence — so far his words. Through this explanation, two difficulties one might raise about the Mishnah are resolved: first, why it enters into a negative formulation; second, the word "better" (tov) — one does not say "better" of one thing than another unless they belong to the same category and are of equal value, and then we say "this is better than that." This resolves everything, for it comes to teach us that a word is worth a sela, [while] silence is worth two — and this is [the meaning of] "I have found nothing for the body better than silence": although speech may be worth as much as a sela, silence is better than it and is worth two — but this does not exclude silence in matters of idle talk and evil speech and the like, for in those cases speech has no value at all, such that we could say silence is better than speech, since there is no equivalence of selas in them — on the contrary, they are blemishing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:37: The pious author, of blessed memory, wrote in his commentary on this Mishnah, in these words: whoever refrains from speaking where he has a need to speak indicates three things about his soul: first, that he is wise — because he is not rash to speak, in the manner of "a coin in a jug rattles, rattles" [a full jug is silent]; second, that his intellect overpowers his materiality, and therefore he restrains his words; third, that he is discerning and his eyes are in his head to foresee the harm liable to come from his words. This is what Solomon said, "He who restrains (chosech) his words has knowledge; a man of understanding has a cool spirit" (Proverbs 17:27) — in saying "restrains," he indicates that he has a need to speak, and yet restrains himself, for this is the common usage of the term — "and I too restrained (va'echsoch)" (Genesis 20:6), "and he has not restrained (chasach) anything from me" (Genesis 39:9). Rabbi Yehudah ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory, likewise wrote this, and he is described with three descriptions: "has knowledge," "cool spirit," "a man of understanding" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:38: It seems to me that these three descriptions correspond to Chochmah, Binah, Da'at — starting with Da'at, which is the essential aspect of the tongue, and then "cool spirit" (yekar ruach), which is the honor of the heart from Chochmah, from where the spirit of life flows; "a man of understanding" corresponds to Binah — and because he holds fast to the place of life, as explained regarding "who is the man who desires life," it is fitting that he be characterized by these three.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:39: The Tanna connects to this and says, "not the study but the deed is the essential thing" — one might connect his words in two ways. First, he comes to tell us that he has taught us this good quality — that he found nothing better for the body than silence — so that the students afterward who call [and study] this quality should not intend to study it and not practice it, lest it be found "fine in preaching but not fine in practice," but that they actually practice and acquire the quality of silence. The same applies to all matters that a person calls [important] that he needs to practice — for "not the study is the essential thing" [but the deed]. The reason he taught us this matter specifically regarding the tongue is that a person's acquisition of this quality requires great effort, because of the tongue's habitual and swift tendency to speak both good and bad; and whoever fulfills this quality will have a key to acquiring the other good qualities that exist, and it is best for him that he study and practice — for once he takes hold of the root and guards it properly, all the branches will endure.
